The present disclosure provides a building information modeling (BIM)-based modular housing system constructed from thin-walled channel steel and comprising foundations, columns, beams, walls, a roof plate, doors, and windows. The columns and transverse beams employ inward-flanged C-section steel or composite square steel formed by symmetrically and oppositely interlocking inward-flanged C-section steel members. Connections between the columns and foundations, the columns and transverse beams, adjacent transverse beams, the columns or transverse beams and slant beams, the transverse beams or slant beams and the roof plate, and the joints of adjacent supports are formed using base connectors, butt connectors, or cross connectors.

According to the technical solution of the present disclosure, inward-flanged C-section steel members, or composite square steel members, can be quickly and securely butt-joined. Each joint is provided with webs and, owing to its high strength, may serve as a standard connector. Relief holes provided on the inner side of the joint interlock with and are pressed against the inward flanges of the inward-flanged C-section steel, thereby creating an internal-external nesting effect. A positioning groove provided on the outer side of the joint interfits with the inward-flanged C-section steel in a concave-convex manner. The assembly is then compressed and secured using a fastening steel strip, thereby providing secure fastening and preventing slippage.

This disclosure describes a BIM-based modular building system made from thin-walled channel steel and including foundations, columns, beams, walls, a roof panel, doors, and windows. The columns and crossbeams are formed either from inward-lipped C-shaped steel sections or from composite square steel members created by symmetrically interlocking two inward-lipped C-shaped sections in opposite orientations.

Base, butt, or cross connectors join the foundations to the columns; the columns to the crossbeams; neighboring crossbeams to one another; the columns or crossbeams to inclined beams; the crossbeams or inclined beams to the roof panel; and adjoining supports at their connection points.

Under the disclosed design, both the inward-lipped C-shaped sections and the composite square steel members can be aligned and connected rapidly and securely. Each joint incorporates webs that provide sufficient strength for it to function as a standardized connector. Relief openings on the inner side of the joint engage the inward-facing lips of the C-shaped steel and are compressed together, producing an internal-and-external nested connection. In addition, an exterior positioning groove interfits with the C-shaped section through complementary recessed and projecting surfaces. A steel fastening strip then compresses and secures the assembly, tightening the connection and preventing slippage.

The disclosure relates to a building information modeling (BIM)-based modular housing system constructed primarily from thin-wall channel steel. The system includes the principal elements required for a complete building, such as foundations, columns, transverse beams, wall assemblies, a roof plate, doors, and windows. BIM may be used to coordinate the design, manufacture, positioning, and assembly of these prefabricated structural components.

The columns and transverse beams are formed from inward-flanging C-section steel. Where greater strength or rigidity is required, two opposing C-sections may be arranged symmetrically and buckled or fastened together to form a combined square-steel member. This configuration provides an efficient, lightweight structural framework suitable for modular production and on-site installation.

Various specialized connectors are used to join the structural members. Depending on the location and orientation of the connection, these may include base connectors, butting connectors, and crossed connectors. Such connectors can be provided at interfaces involving the foundations, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and adjacent supporting members, enabling the different modules and structural elements to be assembled into an integrated load-bearing system.

The joints may incorporate webs to provide high connection strength and stability. Their configuration permits structural members to be connected rapidly and securely, reducing assembly time while maintaining reliable load transfer. Because the joints can be manufactured in standardized forms, they may also serve as universal or standardized connectors for repeated use across different parts of the modular housing system.

Additional features—including relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening steel strips—facilitate accurate alignment and assembly. These elements cooperate to create nested or interlocking connections between adjoining components. The resulting arrangement increases fastening strength, limits relative movement, and helps prevent slippage after installation. Overall, the disclosed system combines standardized thin-wall steel components with reinforced, position-controlled joints to support efficient fabrication and rapid construction of modular housing.
outputs.L4:
The disclosure relates to a building information modeling (BIM)-based modular housing system and an associated assembly method. The system is designed to improve the standardization, manufacturing accuracy, installation speed, and structural reliability of prefabricated housing. A digital BIM model is established for the building and its individual modules so that member dimensions, connector locations, assembly sequences, and material requirements can be coordinated before fabrication. Structural members and connection components can then be manufactured according to the model, transported to the construction site, and assembled in a controlled sequence.

The primary load-bearing framework is formed from thin-wall steel members. Depending on the structural location and design requirements, the members may comprise inward-flanging C-section steel or combined square-steel members assembled from multiple sections. The inward flanges increase local stiffness while providing surfaces suitable for positioning and fastening. Combined square-steel members provide greater resistance to bending, torsion, and local deformation in areas subject to higher loads. The use of standardized steel sections also facilitates factory production and interchangeability among modular components.

Adjacent members are connected by standardized base connectors, butting connectors, and crossed connectors. Base connectors are used to secure vertical or frame members to a supporting foundation, floor structure, or lower module. Butting connectors join members arranged end to end or connect corresponding members of adjacent modules. Crossed connectors are used where members intersect or where loads must be transferred between members extending in different directions. By selecting the appropriate connector type, wall, floor, roof, and corner-frame assemblies can be formed from a limited range of repeatable components.

The joint regions are reinforced at the webs of the steel members to reduce local buckling, tearing, or deformation caused by concentrated connection forces. Reinforcing plates, connector bodies, or other load-distributing elements cooperate with the webs so that forces are transferred more uniformly through the joint. This arrangement improves the strength and rigidity of the connection without requiring excessively thick structural members throughout the entire frame.

The connectors and steel members further include mutually cooperating relief holes and positioning grooves. During assembly, corresponding portions of the connector and member are inserted, overlapped, or interlocked through the relief holes. The positioning grooves guide the components into a predetermined orientation and restrict unintended movement. These features provide preliminary positioning before final fastening, reduce alignment errors, and help maintain the dimensional accuracy specified in the BIM model.

Fastening steel strips are applied at selected connection locations to clamp or lock the assembled members and connectors. The steel strips cooperate with the interlocking holes, grooves, and reinforced webs to resist separation, lateral displacement, and slippage. Mechanical fasteners may be installed after positioning to complete the joint and provide a secure load path between connected components. Because the members are self-locating to a substantial extent, the amount of on-site measuring, temporary bracing, and corrective adjustment can be reduced.

In construction, the BIM model is first used to divide the building into manufacturable and transportable modules and to define each member and joint. The steel members, connectors, reinforcing components, and fastening strips are then fabricated and labeled in accordance with the model. At the site, base connectors are positioned first, after which wall and frame members are installed. Butting connectors join adjacent members or modules, while crossed connectors secure intersecting frame portions. Once the relief holes and positioning grooves are engaged, the fastening steel strips and associated fasteners are installed to lock the joints. The completed modules may then be connected to form the overall housing structure.

The disclosed arrangement combines digital coordination with standardized mechanical connections. It enables rapid and repeatable assembly while reducing dependence on extensive field welding and manual layout. The reinforced and interlocking joint structure provides high connection strength, improves resistance to deformation and slippage, and promotes stable transfer of loads between modules. As a result, the system is suitable for efficient production and erection of modular housing with improved construction quality, structural safety, and dimensional consistency.
outputs.L5:
## The Importance of BIM in Modern Construction

The construction industry increasingly relies on Building Information Modeling (BIM) to plan, design, and manage projects. BIM creates a detailed digital representation of a building, combining information about its structure, materials, costs, and construction schedule.

According to industry professionals, BIM can improve collaboration among architects, engineers, contractors, and clients. Because all participants work with coordinated information, they can identify design conflicts early, reduce costly errors, and make better decisions throughout the project.

The benefits of BIM continue after construction is completed. Building owners can use the digital model to support maintenance, renovations, and facility management. As technology develops, BIM is expected to play an even greater role in creating efficient, sustainable, and cost-effective buildings.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a technical solution for rapidly assembling modular steel housing using BIM, oppositely buckled C-section steel, standardized high-strength joints, relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening steel strips.
counterfactuals.output:
### BIM-Driven Modular Steel Housing System

The proposed solution combines digital design, factory prefabrication, and standardized dry connections to enable rapid assembly and disassembly of low- and mid-rise steel housing.

#### 1. BIM-based design and production

A coordinated BIM model defines:

- Building modules, structural grids, and installation sequence
- Every C-section member, connection plate, bolt, relief hole, positioning groove, and fastening strip
- Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, façade, and interior interfaces
- Part numbers, tolerances, bills of materials, and CNC fabrication files

Rule-based component families ensure that modules and joints remain interchangeable. Clash detection is completed before fabrication, while QR or RFID identifiers link physical parts to BIM installation instructions and quality records.

#### 2. Oppositely buckled C-section members

Two cold-formed C-section steels are placed face-to-face or back-to-back and buckled together in opposite directions. Their interlocking lips and webs form a closed or near-closed box member.

This configuration provides:

- Greater torsional and lateral stability than a single C-section
- Efficient columns, beams, floor edge members, and wall frames
- Nestable parts for economical transport
- Dry fabrication without continuous site welding

The paired sections are secured at calculated intervals with bolts, rivets, clinching, or self-drilling fasteners. Local stiffeners may be added around highly loaded joints.

#### 3. Standardized high-strength joints

A small family of repeatable joints connects columns, beams, floor cassettes, wall panels, and complete volumetric modules. High-strength bolts pass through factory-punched holes into splice plates, end plates, or concealed sleeves.

Typical connections include:

- Column-to-column sleeve joints
- Beam-to-column end-plate joints
- Floor-to-beam bearing and locking joints
- Inter-module corner connections
- Bracing and façade attachment nodes

The joints are designed for one-sided access where possible and use captive nuts or preinstalled threaded plates. This minimizes loose components and allows modules to be replaced or dismantled.

#### 4. Relief holes and positioning grooves

Relief holes are formed near folded corners, interlocking lips, and joint regions. They prevent tearing and distortion during bending, provide bolt or tool clearance, and reduce local stress concentrations. Their size and location are controlled in the BIM fabrication model and checked against structural requirements.

Positioning grooves are pressed or rolled into the C-sections and connection plates. Matching grooves act as self-jigging features: when two members are brought together, the grooves guide them into the correct line, elevation, and orientation before bolting. They also help prevent slip during tightening.

#### 5. Fastening steel strips

Thin galvanized or high-strength steel strips bridge the paired C-sections and lock their open edges together. The strips may slide into positioning grooves or wrap around local connection zones and are fixed by bolts, rivets, or clinched tabs.

They serve several purposes:

- Maintain the geometry of the oppositely buckled sections
- Prevent local opening or separation of the C-sections
- Distribute concentrated joint forces
- Secure wall, floor, ceiling, or service panels
- Provide temporary stability during erection

Strip dimensions and fastening spacing are varied according to the BIM-derived load schedule.

#### 6. Manufacturing and erection sequence

1. Finalize and coordinate the BIM model.
2. Generate CNC cutting, punching, folding, and marking data.
3. Manufacture coded C-sections with relief holes and positioning grooves.
4. Buckle paired sections together and install fastening strips.
5. Assemble wall and floor cassettes or complete room modules in factory jigs.
6. Preinstall services, insulation, windows, and finishes.
7. Transport nested members or completed modules to site.
8. Set modules on prepared foundations using BIM-based survey points.
9. Engage grooves and locating features, install high-strength bolts, and verify torque.
10. Connect services and install façade and weatherproofing components.
11. Update the BIM model with inspection, torque, and as-built data.

The result is a lightweight, dimensionally controlled structural system that reduces site welding, labor, and erection time while improving repeatability, quality assurance, transport efficiency, and future adaptability. Structural resistance, fire protection, corrosion protection, acoustics, progressive-collapse behavior, and joint tolerances must be verified for the applicable building codes and project loads.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a patent-style disclosure explaining how thin-walled channel-steel columns, transverse beams, slant beams, supports, foundations, and roof plates are securely connected in a prefabricated building.
counterfactuals.output:
# PREFABRICATED BUILDING CONNECTION SYSTEM

## Abstract

A prefabricated building connection system is disclosed for securely connecting thin-walled channel-steel columns, transverse beams, slant beams, diagonal supports, foundations, and roof plates. Each column is fixed to a foundation by a base connector including a base plate, anchor bolts, and an upwardly projecting column-receiving member. Transverse beams are connected to the columns by bolted seat brackets and side plates that restrain vertical, lateral, and rotational movement. Slant beams are connected to the columns and transverse beams through gusset assemblies having overlapping bearing surfaces and aligned fastener openings. Diagonal supports extend between selected columns, beams, or foundation connectors and are fastened by reinforced gusset plates. Roof plates are secured to the slant beams by clips or self-drilling fasteners having weather-sealing members. The connections are principally mechanical and are accessible from the exterior of the structural members, thereby facilitating rapid field assembly while limiting deformation of the thin-walled channel sections.

## Technical Field

The disclosure relates to prefabricated light-steel buildings and, more particularly, to connection structures for joining thin-walled channel-steel framing members to one another, to a foundation, and to roof-covering plates.

## Background

Thin-walled channel-steel members are suitable for prefabricated buildings because they are lightweight, dimensionally consistent, and readily transported. However, direct field welding or fastening through unsupported channel walls may cause local buckling, tearing, distortion, or fastener pull-through. Conventional connections may also require access to both sides of a member or may not adequately transfer uplift, lateral, and rotational loads.

Accordingly, there is a need for a prefabricated connection system that distributes connection forces over reinforced portions of the channel-steel members, accommodates manufacturing and foundation tolerances, permits rapid bolted assembly, and provides a continuous load path from the roof plates to the foundation.

## Summary of the Disclosure

A prefabricated building system includes:

1. a plurality of foundations;
2. thin-walled channel-steel columns secured to the foundations by base connector assemblies;
3. transverse beams connected between adjacent columns by beam connector assemblies;
4. slant beams connected to upper portions of the columns or transverse beams by roof-frame connector assemblies;
5. diagonal supports connected by gusset assemblies between selected structural members; and
6. roof plates mechanically fastened to the slant beams.

At locations at which a concentrated connection force is introduced into a thin-walled channel member, the member preferably includes one or more reinforcing plates, channel sleeves, spacer blocks, or crush-resistant inserts. Such reinforcement prevents opposing channel walls from collapsing when the fasteners are tightened and spreads the applied load along the member.

The primary connections are preferably made with bolts, locknuts, self-locking pins, or other removable mechanical fasteners. Welding may be performed under controlled factory conditions to attach brackets, end plates, or reinforcement pieces, while field assembly may be completed substantially without welding.

## Brief Description of Exemplary Figures

- **FIG. 1** is a perspective view of an assembled prefabricated building frame.
- **FIG. 2** is an exploded view of a column-to-foundation connection.
- **FIG. 3** is an exploded view of a transverse-beam-to-column connection.
- **FIG. 4** is a side view of an eave connection between a column and a slant beam.
- **FIG. 5** is a view of a ridge connection between opposed slant beams.
- **FIG. 6** is a view of a diagonal-support connection.
- **FIG. 7** is a cross-sectional view of a roof-plate connection.

## Detailed Description

### 1. General Frame Arrangement

Referring generally to **FIG. 1**, a building frame **100** includes foundations **110**, upright columns **120**, transverse beams **130**, slant beams **140**, diagonal supports **150**, and roof plates **160**.

Each column **120**, transverse beam **130**, slant beam **140**, and support **150** may be formed from cold-formed, thin-walled channel steel having a web and two side flanges. The flanges may include inwardly turned lips for increased stiffness. In selected embodiments, two channel members are arranged back-to-back to form a built-up member. The built-up members may be joined at spaced intervals by bolts, rivets, clinched fasteners, or factory welds.

Connection openings may be punched or drilled at the factory according to a common modular spacing. The openings may include circular holes for fixed positioning and elongated holes for assembly tolerance or thermal movement.

### 2. Column-to-Foundation Connection

Each foundation **110** may comprise a concrete footing, pier, slab thickening, ground screw, or precast foundation block. A plurality of anchor elements **112** are secured within or to the foundation. In a concrete embodiment, the anchor elements are threaded anchor rods embedded in the concrete and connected to an anchor cage or reinforcing bars.

A base connector assembly **170** includes:

- a horizontal base plate **172** supported on the foundation;
- anchor openings receiving the anchor elements **112**;
- an upwardly projecting column-receiving portion **174**; and
- one or more stiffening ribs **176** extending between the base plate and the column-receiving portion.

The column-receiving portion **174** may be a channel-shaped socket positioned around the lower end of the column **120**, or a blade or sleeve received inside the column. The lower end of the column includes aligned bolt openings. Bolts **178** extend through the column walls and the column-receiving portion.

A tubular spacer, solid spacer block, folded reinforcing plate, or internal sleeve **180** is positioned between opposing wall portions of the column at each bolt location. Tightening the bolts therefore clamps the connection without crushing the thin-walled section.

The base plate **172** may include oversized or elongated anchor openings to accommodate positional tolerances. After alignment, leveling nuts, shims, or non-shrink grout **182** are provided beneath the base plate. Upper anchor nuts are then tightened to clamp the base plate against the foundation.

The upwardly projecting portion **174** transfers shear and bending forces, while the anchor elements **112** resist uplift and overturning. Drainage openings may be formed in the base connector to prevent water accumulation. Exposed surfaces may be galvanized or provided with a corrosion-resistant coating.

### 3. Transverse-Beam-to-Column Connection

Each transverse beam **130** extends between adjacent columns **120**. A beam connector assembly **200** is provided at each end of the transverse beam.

In one embodiment, the connector assembly **200** includes a seat bracket **202** attached to the column. The seat bracket has:

- a horizontal or generally horizontal bearing flange **204** supporting the lower edge of the beam;
- a vertical attachment flange **206** fastened to the column; and
- opposed side flanges **208** engaging respective sides of the beam.

The beam end rests on the bearing flange so that gravity loads are transmitted by direct bearing rather than solely through the fasteners. Bolts **210** extend through the side flanges, the beam web or flanges, and reinforcing inserts **212** located within the beam.

An upper retaining plate **214** overlaps the beam and the column. The retaining plate resists uplift and limits rotation of the beam relative to the column. The seat bracket and retaining plate may be separate components or portions of a single folded-steel connector.

Where the transverse beam is connected to a channel column having an open side, a backing plate **216** may be positioned within the channel. Bolts clamp the seat bracket, column wall, and backing plate together. The backing plate distributes the bolt force and reduces localized bearing stress.

In another embodiment, an end plate is factory-attached to the transverse beam. The end plate overlaps the web or flanges of the column and is bolted to a reinforced region of the column. A lower tab on the end plate enters a corresponding slot in the column or seat bracket. The tab temporarily supports and locates the beam during installation before the bolts are inserted.

### 4. Column-to-Slant-Beam Eave Connection

The slant beams **140** form roof rafters and extend upwardly from the columns toward a roof ridge. At each eave, an eave connector assembly **230** joins a lower end of a slant beam to an upper portion of a column.

The eave connector assembly includes a gusset plate **232** having a first region overlapping the column and a second region overlapping the slant beam. The first and second regions are angularly oriented according to the intended roof pitch. The gusset plate may be located on one side of the frame member, or paired gusset plates may be located on opposite sides.

A lower edge or folded flange **234** of the gusset plate forms a bearing seat for the slant beam. Bolts **236** extend through the gusset plate, the reinforced upper portion of the column, and the reinforced end portion of the slant beam. At least some of the bolt openings may be elongated to permit pitch adjustment before final tightening.

An angular stop surface **238** bears against the end of the slant beam. Compression loads are thereby transmitted through bearing surfaces, while the bolts principally resist separation, uplift, and shear. Reinforcing sleeves or nested channel sections are positioned within the column and slant beam at the connection.

The upper end of the column may additionally be tied to the transverse beam **130**, forming a multi-member eave node. In such an arrangement, a common gusset assembly overlaps the column, transverse beam, and slant beam to provide a continuous connection among all three members.

### 5. Ridge Connection Between Slant Beams

Opposed slant beams **140** meet at the roof ridge. A ridge connector assembly **250** includes paired ridge plates **252** positioned on opposite sides of the slant beams. The ridge plates include inclined portions conforming to the roof pitch and a central portion spanning the joint.

Bolts **254** pass through the ridge plates and reinforced end portions of the slant beams. The ends of the slant beams may bear against one another or against a central ridge block **256**. The ridge block maintains the desired spacing and prevents inward deformation when the bolts are tightened.

A ridge purlin or longitudinal member may be supported by an upwardly projecting flange of the ridge connector. The ridge connector may also include openings for attaching roof-plate closures or ridge caps.

### 6. Diagonal Support Connections

Diagonal supports **150** brace the building against wind, seismic, and assembly loads. A support may extend:

- between a lower portion of a column and a transverse beam;
- between a column and a slant beam;
- between adjacent columns;
- between adjacent roof-frame members; or
- between a column and the base connector assembly.

Each end of a support **150** includes a flattened end portion, clevis, end plate, or threaded end fitting **270**. The end fitting is connected to a gusset plate **272** by one or more bolts or pins **274**.

The gusset plate is fastened to a reinforced portion of the corresponding column, beam, slant beam, or base connector. Preferably, the support fastener axis and the principal axis of the support substantially intersect, thereby limiting eccentric loading.

In an adjustable embodiment, the support includes oppositely threaded end portions and a central turnbuckle body **276**. Rotation of the turnbuckle body changes the effective support length, enabling the frame to be squared and pre-tensioned. Locknuts prevent unintended rotation after adjustment.

Where crossed supports are used, the supports may pass one another without direct contact or may be joined by a central spacer and bolt. Tension-only straps may alternatively be used in opposed pairs.

### 7. Roof-Plate Connection

The roof plates **160** may comprise corrugated, ribbed, standing-seam, or substantially planar metal panels. The plates are laid over the slant beams **140** or over longitudinal purlins connected to the slant beams.

In a directly fastened embodiment, self-drilling screws **290** pass through raised portions of the roof plates and into an upper flange of the slant beam or purlin. Each screw includes a metal load-distributing washer and an elastomeric sealing washer **292**. A reinforcing strip may be positioned below the roof plate to increase resistance to wind uplift.

In a concealed-fastener embodiment, clips **294** are fastened to the slant beams or purlins. Edge portions of adjacent roof plates interlock with the clips and with one another. At least some clips permit limited sliding movement in the direction of the roof slope, thereby accommodating thermal expansion without loosening the connection.

Adjacent roof plates overlap by at least one rib or by a prescribed edge distance. A compressible sealing strip **296** is disposed within the overlap. Stitch screws or seam fasteners secure the overlapping edges independently of the main structural fasteners.

At the eaves, a closure member and drip flashing are secured beneath the roof plates. At the ridge, opposed roof plates are covered by a ridge cap attached to the ridge connector or to closure members. Sealing gaskets prevent water intrusion through the connection openings.

### 8. Reinforcement of Thin-Walled Members

To prevent failure of the thin-walled channel sections, each high-load connection may include one or more of the following:

- an internal nested channel having a shape complementary to the main member;
- a backing plate engaging the channel web;
- a spacer extending between opposing flanges;
- a tubular crush sleeve surrounding a bolt;
- a folded plate engaging the web and both flanges;
- a load-distributing washer having an enlarged bearing area; or
- a local bead, rib, embossment, or hem formed in the channel wall.

The reinforcement extends beyond the outermost fastener by a sufficient distance to distribute bearing and tear-out forces. Fastener openings are preferably spaced from free edges and bends of the channel member.

### 9. Assembly Procedure

An exemplary assembly method includes:

1. installing the foundation anchor elements and locating the base plates;
2. leveling and temporarily securing the base connector assemblies;
3. placing the columns over or around the column-receiving portions;
4. inserting and tightening the column fasteners;
5. positioning the transverse beams on the seat brackets and installing the beam fasteners;
6. attaching the slant beams to the eave and ridge connector assemblies;
7. installing diagonal supports and adjusting the supports until the frame is plumb and square;
8. finally tightening the structural fasteners to a specified preload;
9. installing purlins, when used;
10. fastening the roof plates and weather-sealing components; and
11. applying grout, protective caps, sealant, or corrosion-repair coating as required.

Temporary locating tabs, hooks, or slots may support each member during assembly, allowing an installer to release lifting equipment before all final fasteners are installed.

## Advantages

The disclosed arrangement provides:

- a continuous load path from the roof plates through the slant beams, transverse beams, columns, and base connectors to the foundations;
- bearing-supported beam and rafter connections rather than fastener-only suspension;
- resistance to uplift, shear, bending, and rotational movement;
- reduced risk of crushing or tearing thin-walled channel members;
- rapid, substantially weld-free field assembly;
- replaceable and demountable structural components;
- tolerance adjustment at the foundation and frame connections; and
- weather-resistant roof fastening with provision for thermal movement.

## Exemplary Claims

1. **A prefabricated building system**, comprising:  
   a foundation having a plurality of anchor elements;  
   a base connector secured to the foundation by the anchor elements;  
   a thin-walled channel-steel column received by the base connector and mechanically fastened thereto;  
   a transverse beam connected to the column by a connector having a bearing seat and at least one side plate;  
   a slant beam connected to an upper portion of the column by a gusset assembly;  
   a diagonal support connected between two structural members by reinforced gusset plates; and  
   a roof plate mechanically secured to the slant beam or to a purlin supported by the slant beam,  
   wherein at least one connection includes an internal reinforcement that resists deformation of a thin-walled channel section when a mechanical fastener is tightened.

2. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the base connector includes a base plate, an upwardly projecting column-receiving portion, and a stiffening rib extending therebetween.

3. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the transverse beam is supported vertically by the bearing seat and is restrained against uplift by an upper retaining plate.

4. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the gusset assembly includes an angular bearing surface engaging an end portion of the slant beam.

5. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the internal reinforcement comprises a spacer sleeve disposed around a bolt and extending between opposing wall portions of the channel section.

6. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the diagonal support includes a threaded length-adjustment member configured to square and pre-tension the building frame.

7. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the roof plate is attached by a self-drilling fastener having a load-distributing washer and an elastomeric sealing washer.

8. The prefabricated building system of claim 1, wherein the roof plate is attached by a concealed clip configured to permit thermal sliding of the roof plate.

9. **A method of assembling a prefabricated building**, comprising:  
   anchoring base connectors to foundations;  
   mechanically fastening channel-steel columns to the base connectors;  
   placing transverse beams on bearing seats attached to the columns;  
   bolting the transverse beams to reinforced portions of the columns;  
   connecting slant beams to upper portions of the columns using angular gusset assemblies;  
   connecting diagonal supports to the frame and adjusting the supports to align the frame; and  
   mechanically securing roof plates to the slant beams or to purlins supported by the slant beams.

10. The method of claim 9, further comprising inserting crush-resistant spacers into the channel-steel members before tightening bolts through the members.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an English patent summary for a modular housing invention in which inward-flanged C-section steel members are joined through internal-external nesting, concave-convex positioning, and steel-strip fastening to prevent slippage.
counterfactuals.output: A modular housing system is disclosed in which prefabricated structural modules are assembled using inward-flanged C-section steel members. Adjacent steel members are connected by internal-external nesting, with one member received at least partially within another. Complementary concave and convex positioning portions engage to align the members and restrict relative transverse and rotational movement. One or more steel fastening strips extend across or around the nested connection and are secured to the steel members, thereby retaining the engagement and preventing longitudinal slippage or separation. The connection structure enables rapid, accurate assembly while improving joint stability, load transfer, and resistance to deformation. The system is suitable for modular walls, floors, roofs, frames, and inter-module connections, and facilitates prefabrication, transportation, on-site installation, disassembly, and reuse.
